topics.title: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: Name the five countries that neighbour Uganda and give the direction of each.
questions.a: Kenya — east; South Sudan — north; D.R. Congo — west; Rwanda — south-west; Tanzania — south.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: What is a compass used for? Name the four cardinal and four semi-cardinal points.
questions.a: A compass is used to find direction. Cardinal: North, East, South, West. Semi-cardinal: North-East, South-East, South-West, North-West.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: Define lines of latitude and lines of longitude.
questions.a: Lines of latitude are imaginary lines running from west to east, showing distance north or south of the Equator. Lines of longitude run from the North Pole to the South Pole, showing distance east or west of the Prime Meridian.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: Which line of latitude passes through Uganda, and what does it do to the country?
questions.a: The Equator. It divides Uganda so that part of the country lies in the Northern Hemisphere and part in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: Between which lines of latitude and longitude does Uganda lie?
questions.a: Between about 4°N and 1°S, and between about 29°E and 35°E.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: Why is Uganda called a landlocked country, and which two ports does it use?
questions.a: Because it has no coastline of its own. It uses the ports of Mombasa in Kenya and Dar es Salaam in Tanzania.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: Name the five elements of a map.
questions.a: Title, key, scale, compass (direction) and frame.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: Give the use of a key and of a scale on a map.
questions.a: The key explains the symbols used on the map; the scale shows how distance on the map compares with distance on the ground.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: On a map of scale 1 : 50,000, two towns are 8 cm apart. Find the real distance.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: How is a grid reference read?
questions.a: Read the eastings (the lines going across) first, then the northings (the lines going up).

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: What is the capital city of Uganda, and where is the international airport?
questions.a: The capital is Kampala; the international airport is at Entebbe.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: About how big is Uganda, and about how much of it is water and swamp?
questions.a: About 241,000 km², and about one fifth of it is open water and swamp.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: Name the four regions of Uganda.
questions.a: Central, Eastern, Northern and Western.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: Give one reason why the number of districts in Uganda keeps changing.
questions.a: Because government creates new districts by splitting the old ones, to bring services nearer to the people.

questions.subject: SST
questions.topic: Location of Uganda on the Map of East Africa
questions.q: Draw the map of Uganda showing the Equator, Kampala and the neighbouring countries.
questions.a: Learner's map. It should show Uganda with the Equator crossing the south, Kampala marked near Lake Victoria, and the five neighbours named in their correct positions.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What are physical features? Name any six found in Uganda.
questions.a: Physical features are the natural land forms found on the earth's surface. Any six of: mountains, hills, plateaux, plains, rift valleys, lakes, rivers, waterfalls, swamps, islands.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name the highest mountain in Uganda, its highest peak and its height.
questions.a: Mt Rwenzori; its highest peak is Margherita, about 5,109 metres high.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any three volcanic mountains in Uganda and say where each is.
questions.a: Any three: Mt Elgon — Mbale in the east; Muhavura — Kisoro in the south-west; Moroto — Karamoja in the north-east (also Kadam, Napak).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give the difference between a block mountain and a volcanic mountain, with one Ugandan example of each.
questions.a: A block mountain is formed when land between two faults is pushed up or the sides sink, for example Rwenzori; a volcanic mountain is formed when molten rock comes out of the earth, cools and piles up, for example Elgon.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is a rift valley? Name three lakes found in Uganda's rift valley.
questions.a: A rift valley is a deep, wide valley formed when the land between two faults sinks. Lakes: Albert, Edward and George.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any five lakes in Uganda and say how each type was formed.
questions.a: Any five, for example: Victoria and Kyoga — down-warping; Albert, Edward and George — faulting; Katwe — volcanic (crater); a lake behind a dam — man-made.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is a crater lake? Give one example in Uganda.
questions.a: A crater lake is a lake formed in the mouth of an old volcano. Example: Lake Katwe (also Nyamunuka).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Trace the course of the River Nile through Uganda, naming its two parts.
questions.a: The Nile leaves Lake Victoria at Jinja as the Victoria Nile, flows through Lake Kyoga, over Murchison Falls into Lake Albert, and then flows north as the Albert Nile into South Sudan.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any four waterfalls in Uganda and the rivers on which they are found.
questions.a: Any four: Murchison (Kabalega) Falls and Karuma Falls — the Victoria Nile; Bujagali and Owen Falls — the Nile near Jinja; Sipi Falls — the River Sipi on Mt Elgon.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any three islands of Uganda.
questions.a: Any three of: the Ssese Islands, Buvuma, Koome (all in Lake Victoria).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five ways in which physical features help the people of Uganda.
questions.a: Any five of: mountains give relief rainfall and fertile soils; lakes and rivers give water, fish and transport; rivers give hydro-electric power; features attract tourists; swamps give papyrus, clay and water; they form natural boundaries.
accepted: mountains give relief rainfall and fertile soils

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four problems caused by physical features.
questions.a: Any four of: mountains make road building hard; steep slopes cause soil erosion and landslides; rivers and lakes flood; swamps breed mosquitoes and bilharzia snails; some areas are cut off in the rains.
accepted: steep slopes cause soil erosion and landslides
swamps breed mosquitoes and bilharzia snails
some areas are cut off in the rains

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why do landslides happen at Bududa, and how can they be prevented?
questions.a: Because people have cleared the trees and farm on very steep slopes on Mt Elgon, so heavy rain loosens the bare soil and it slides. Prevention: plant trees and grass on the slopes, dig terraces and contour trenches, avoid cultivating very steep land, and resettle people from dangerous slopes.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five ways of caring for physical features.
questions.a: Any five of: plant trees on hills and river banks; dig terraces and contour trenches; do not build or farm in swamps; do not pour waste into lakes and rivers; avoid bush burning; restore quarried land; obey environmental laws.
accepted: plant trees on hills and river banks
do not pour waste into lakes and rivers

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the map of Uganda and mark on it Mt Rwenzori, Lake Victoria and Murchison Falls.
questions.a: Learner's map. Rwenzori in the west, Lake Victoria in the south, and Murchison Falls on the Victoria Nile in the north-west.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give the difference between weather and climate.
questions.a: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular time, while climate is the average weather of a place over a long period, usually 30 years or more.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any five elements of weather and the instrument used to measure each.
questions.a: Any five: rainfall — rain gauge; temperature — thermometer; wind direction — wind vane; wind speed — anemometer; humidity — hygrometer; air pressure — barometer; sunshine — sunshine recorder.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is a Stevenson screen, and why is it painted white?
questions.a: A Stevenson screen is the white wooden box in which weather instruments are kept at a weather station. It is painted white to reflect heat, so the readings are not affected by the sun.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name the climatic regions of Uganda and describe any two.
questions.a: Equatorial (wet), tropical (savannah), semi-arid and montane. (Describe any two, for example: the equatorial region has rain almost all year, over 1,200 mm, and is warm and humid; the semi-arid region has under 750 mm of unreliable rain, long dry spells and very high temperatures.)

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Which part of Uganda is the wettest, and which is the driest?
questions.a: The wettest is the Lake Victoria basin and the south-west; the driest is Karamoja.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five factors that influence the climate of Uganda.
questions.a: Any five of: altitude, nearness to water bodies, relief, vegetation, winds, latitude, human activities.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why is it cold in Kabale and on the Rwenzori Mountains?
questions.a: Because they lie at a high altitude, and temperature falls by about 1 °C for every 150 metres you climb.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Explain how Lake Victoria influences the climate of the areas near it.
questions.a: Water evaporates from the lake and forms clouds, so the areas near it receive more rainfall; the lake also cools the air by day and warms it at night, giving a moderate temperature.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is relief rainfall, and what is a rain shadow?
questions.a: Relief rainfall is rain formed when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain, cools and condenses. A rain shadow is the dry leeward side of the mountain, which receives little rain.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give three activities favoured by the wet equatorial region.
questions.a: Any three of: growing coffee, bananas, sugar cane, tea or vanilla; fishing; lumbering.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give two activities carried out in the semi-arid region of Karamoja and say why.
questions.a: Nomadic pastoralism, because the pasture and water are scattered and seasonal, so herders move to find them; and growing drought-resistant crops such as sorghum and millet, because the rainfall is too little for crops that need much water.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five problems associated with climate in Uganda.
questions.a: Any five of: drought and famine, floods, landslides, hailstorms and lightning, soil erosion, unreliable rainfall, crop pests and diseases.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give a solution to each of: drought, floods, landslides, soil erosion.
questions.a: Drought — irrigation and water harvesting; floods — drainage channels and not building in wetlands; landslides — terracing, planting trees and avoiding steep slopes; soil erosion — contour ploughing, mulching and cover crops.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four human activities that are changing the climate of Uganda.
questions.a: Any four of: cutting down forests; draining swamps; bush burning; smoke from factories and vehicles; overgrazing; quarrying and mining.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Suggest any four ways of protecting the climate of Uganda.
questions.a: Any four of: plant trees (afforestation and reafforestation); protect wetlands and forest reserves; use energy-saving stoves, biogas and solar; stop bush burning; teach people about the environment; enforce environmental laws.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is vegetation? Give the two main types with two examples of each.
questions.a: Vegetation is the general plant cover of an area. Natural vegetation grows on its own — forests and swamps; planted vegetation is planted by people — plantations and woodlots.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any four types of natural vegetation found in Uganda and where each is found.
questions.a: Any four: tropical rain forest — Mabira, Budongo, Bwindi; savannah — central and northern Uganda; semi-desert — Karamoja; montane — Rwenzori and Elgon slopes; swamp vegetation — around Lakes Kyoga and Victoria.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any four natural forests in Uganda and the districts where they are.
questions.a: Any four: Mabira — Buikwe; Budongo — Masindi; Bwindi — Kanungu; Kibale — Kabarole; Mpanga — Mpigi.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Describe how vegetation changes as you climb Mt Rwenzori.
questions.a: It changes in bands: forest at the bottom, then bamboo, then heath, then moorland, and finally bare rock, ice and snow at the top, because it becomes colder as you climb.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five factors that influence the distribution of vegetation in Uganda.
questions.a: Any five of: rainfall, temperature, soil type, relief and altitude, drainage, human activities.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why does thick forest grow around Lake Victoria but not in Karamoja?
questions.a: Because the area around Lake Victoria receives heavy, reliable rainfall and has deep fertile soils, which support tall trees, while Karamoja is semi-arid, with under 750 mm of unreliable rain, so only short grass and thorn bushes can survive.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six importances of vegetation.
questions.a: Any six of: timber, poles, firewood and charcoal; herbal medicine and wild foods; pasture; attracting rainfall; preventing soil erosion; a home for wild animals; attracting tourists; raw materials for industry; filtering water in wetlands; shade and beauty.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give three uses of papyrus from the swamps.
questions.a: Making mats, baskets and hats; thatching and fencing; and making crafts for sale (papyrus also filters water and provides mulch).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Which vegetation zones are densely populated, and why?
questions.a: The savannah, the Lake Victoria crescent and the lower mountain slopes, because they have good rainfall, fertile soils and land that is easy to clear and farm.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Which vegetation zones are sparsely populated, and why?
questions.a: Thick forests (hard to clear, poor leached soils, pests), semi-desert Karamoja (too dry) and swamps (waterlogged, mosquitoes, hard to build on).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five effects of a growing population on vegetation.
questions.a: Any five of: deforestation for farmland and firewood; swamp reclamation; overgrazing; bush burning; soil erosion and loss of fertility; loss of wildlife habitats; disappearance of some plant species.
accepted: soil erosion and loss of fertility

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give the difference between afforestation and reafforestation.
questions.a: Afforestation is planting trees in an area where there were none before; reafforestation is replanting trees where they were cut down.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six ways of conserving vegetation.
questions.a: Any six of: afforestation and reafforestation; agroforestry; energy-saving stoves, biogas and solar; gazetting forest reserves and parks; protecting wetlands and river banks; controlled grazing and burning; public education; enforcing laws.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name the two bodies that protect Uganda's forests and environment.
questions.a: The National Forestry Authority (NFA) and the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the map of Uganda and shade Mabira Forest, the Karamoja dry area and Bwindi Forest.
questions.a: Learner's map. Mabira in the centre near Jinja, Karamoja in the north-east, and Bwindi in the far south-west.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What are natural resources? Name any six found in Uganda.
questions.a: Natural resources are useful things provided by nature which people use to satisfy their needs. Any six of: land and soil, water, minerals, forests and vegetation, wildlife, climate, people.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name the mineral mined at each of: Kilembe, Hima, Katwe, Busia.
questions.a: Kilembe — copper; Hima — limestone; Katwe — salt; Busia — gold.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Where was oil discovered in Uganda, and give one use of it.
questions.a: In the Albertine Graben (around Hoima and Buliisa). It is used to make fuel such as petrol, diesel and paraffin, and it earns the country money.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give the difference between open cast and shaft mining, with a Ugandan example of each.
questions.a: Open cast mining removes the soil above the mineral and scoops it out, for example limestone at Hima; shaft mining sinks deep shafts and tunnels underground, for example copper at Kilembe.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five uses of water as a natural resource.
questions.a: Any five of: drinking and domestic use; irrigation; fishing; transport; hydro-electric power; tourism; watering animals; industry.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any four hydro-electric power stations in Uganda.
questions.a: Any four of: Nalubaale, Kiira, Bujagali, Isimba, Karuma.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five ways in which natural resources help the economy of Uganda.
questions.a: Any five of: they earn foreign exchange; they create employment; they give government taxes and royalties; they supply raw materials for industries; they lead to building of roads and towns; they raise people's incomes.
accepted: they give government taxes and royalties
they supply raw materials for industries
they lead to building of roads and towns

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why are people also called a natural resource?
questions.a: Because the people supply the labour and skills needed to use every other resource, they pay taxes, and they form the market that buys the goods produced.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six problems faced in developing Uganda's natural resources.
questions.a: Any six of: shortage of capital; low technology and few skilled people; poor transport; small scattered deposits; unstable world prices; pollution; land disputes; corruption and smuggling; pests, diseases and drought; over-exploitation.
accepted: low technology and few skilled people

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six bad practices that destroy natural resources.
questions.a: Any six of: deforestation; bush burning; swamp draining; over-fishing and use of poison or wrong nets; poaching; overgrazing; over-cultivation; mining without restoring land; pouring waste into water; careless use of chemicals.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five ways of caring for the soil.
questions.a: Any five of: crop rotation, mulching, terracing, contour ploughing, applying manure, planting cover crops, fallowing, controlled grazing.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four ways of protecting fish in Uganda's lakes.
questions.a: Any four of: using the recommended net sizes; observing closed seasons; banning poison and explosives; encouraging fish farming; patrolling the lakes; removing water hyacinth.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name the three government bodies that protect the environment, forests and wildlife.
questions.a: NEMA (environment), the National Forestry Authority (NFA) and the Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why is it better to process minerals in Uganda than to export them raw?
questions.a: Because processing adds value, so the goods sell at a much higher price; it also creates jobs at home, supplies local industries, and saves the country from depending on unstable raw-material prices.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the map of Uganda and mark Kilembe, Tororo and Lake Katwe.
questions.a: Learner's map. Kilembe in the west near the Rwenzori, Tororo in the east, and Lake Katwe in the western rift valley.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is an ethnic group? Name the four major ethnic groups of Uganda.
questions.a: An ethnic group is a large group of people who share the same origin, language family and customs. The four are the Bantu, the Luo (River–Lake Nilotes), the Nilo-Hamites (Plain Nilotes) and the Hamites (Cushites).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give the cradle land of each of the four groups.
questions.a: Bantu — Central and West Africa; Luo — Bahr-el-Ghazal, South Sudan; Nilo-Hamites — Ethiopia; Hamites — North-East Africa.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any three tribes in each of the Bantu and Luo groups.
questions.a: Bantu: Baganda, Banyankole, Bagisu (also Banyoro, Batooro, Bakiga, Basoga). Luo: Acholi, Langi, Alur (also Japadhola).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five reasons why the ethnic groups migrated into Uganda.
questions.a: Any five of: search for fertile land and pasture; population pressure; wars and conflicts; drought and famine; diseases and pests; the wish to expand; following their cattle.
accepted: search for fertile land and pasture

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four problems they met during their migration.
questions.a: Any four of: resistance from people already there; wild animals; diseases; thick forests, rivers and swamps; shortage of food and water; long distances; language barriers.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four effects of the migrations on Uganda.
questions.a: Any four of: population increased; new skills such as iron working and farming spread; intermarriage created new communities; kingdoms and chiefdoms were formed; wars broke out over land; some peoples lost their land and culture.
accepted: new skills such as iron working and farming spread
some peoples lost their land and culture

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is a clan, and what is a totem?
questions.a: A clan is a group of related families with a common ancestor. A totem is an animal or plant respected by a clan, which members never eat or kill.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five features of the social organisation of pre-colonial Uganda.
questions.a: Any five of: people lived in clans with totems; the extended family lived and worked together; marriage was arranged between clans with bride price; they believed in a supreme god, spirits and ancestors; they held ceremonies such as naming, initiation and burial rites; education was informal, through work, folk tales and proverbs.
accepted: people lived in clans with totems
the extended family lived and worked together
marriage was arranged between clans with bride price
they believed in a supreme god
they held ceremonies such as naming

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give the difference between a centralised and a decentralised society, with two examples of each.
questions.a: A centralised society is ruled by one leader such as a king, for example Buganda and Bunyoro; a decentralised society has no single ruler and is led by clan elders, for example the Acholi and the Karimojong.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name the traditional titles of the rulers of Buganda, Bunyoro, Ankole and Busoga.
questions.a: Buganda — Kabaka; Bunyoro — Omukama; Ankole — Omugabe; Busoga — Kyabazinga.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Describe how the kingdom of Buganda was governed.
questions.a: The Kabaka was the head. He was helped by the Katikkiro (prime minister) and the Lukiiko (council). Below them were county (Ssaza), sub-county (Ggombolola) and parish (Muluka) chiefs, who collected tribute, kept order, settled cases and raised the army.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: How were decisions made in a decentralised society?
questions.a: By discussion and agreement among the clan elders, who settled disputes, shared out land, led ceremonies and organised defence; there was no single king to decide for everyone.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six economic activities of pre-colonial Uganda.
questions.a: Any six of: crop growing; cattle keeping; iron working; bark cloth making; pottery and basketry; salt making; fishing; hunting; barter trade.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is barter trade, and what was used as money before coins?
questions.a: Barter trade is exchanging goods for goods without using money. Before coins, people used cowrie shells as money.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the map of Uganda and shade the areas settled by the Bantu and the Luo.
questions.a: Learner's map. The Bantu areas should cover the south, west and parts of the east; the Luo areas the north and north-west.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any four groups of foreigners who came to Uganda and say where each came from.
questions.a: Any four: Arab traders — from Arabia in Asia; Indian traders — from India; European explorers — from Europe; missionaries — from Europe; colonial administrators — from Britain.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Who was the first Arab to reach Buganda, when, and during whose reign?
questions.a: Ahmed bin Ibrahim, in about 1844, during the reign of Kabaka Suna II.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What did the Arabs bring, and what did they take away?
questions.a: They brought guns, gunpowder, cloth, carpets, cowrie shells, beads and mirrors, and they took away ivory, slaves, gold, salt and animal skins.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give two positive and two negative effects of the Arab traders.
questions.a: Positive: trade grew and cowrie shells became money; Islam was introduced. Negative: the slave trade took away many people; guns spread and increased wars.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Which two explorers reached the source of the Nile, and in which year?
questions.a: John Hanning Speke and James Grant, in 1862.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What did Sir Samuel Baker reach in 1864?
questions.a: Lake Albert and Murchison Falls.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Who wrote the letter that invited missionaries to Buganda, and in which year?
questions.a: Henry Morton Stanley, in 1875.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name the two missionary groups, the years they came, and one leader of each.
questions.a: The CMS (Protestants) came in 1877 — Rev. Shergold Smith (or Rev. C. T. Wilson); the White Fathers (Catholics) came in 1879 — Fr. Simeon Lourdel, called Mapeera (or Bro. Amans).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four things the missionaries did in Uganda.
questions.a: Any four of: built churches; started schools; built hospitals; translated the Bible and wrote down local languages; introduced new crops and skills; fought the slave trade; trained teachers and nurses.
accepted: translated the Bible and wrote down local languages

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Who are the Uganda Martyrs, and when are they remembered?
questions.a: They are the young Christian converts killed at Namugongo in 1885–1887 during the reign of Kabaka Mwanga. They are remembered every 3rd June, when pilgrims go to Namugongo.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four reasons why the explorers came to Uganda.
questions.a: Any four of: to find the source of the Nile; to map the interior; to look for raw materials and markets; for adventure and fame; to see how the slave trade could be stopped.
accepted: to find the source of the Nile
to look for raw materials and markets
to see how the slave trade could be stopped

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five problems the explorers faced.
questions.a: Any five of: tropical diseases; hostile people; wild animals; thick forests, swamps and rivers; language barriers; shortage of food and clean water; desertion by porters; long distances.
accepted: shortage of food and clean water

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: In which year did Uganda become a British Protectorate, and what was the 1900 Buganda Agreement?
questions.a: 1894. The 1900 Buganda Agreement was signed between Sir Harry Johnston and the Buganda regents; it divided land into mailo and Crown land, fixed taxes, and set out how Buganda would be governed under British protection.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six positive effects of foreign influence in Uganda.
questions.a: Any six of: Christianity and Islam were introduced; schools and hospitals were built; roads and the railway were built; new cash crops were introduced; the slave trade was stopped; trade and money replaced barter; local languages were written down; the peoples were joined into one country.
accepted: roads and the railway were built
the peoples were joined into one country

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six negative effects of foreign influence in Uganda.
questions.a: Any six of: Uganda lost its independence; forced labour and heavy taxes; land was taken; traditional rulers lost power; African culture and religion were despised; religious wars broke out; new diseases came; raw materials were exploited.
accepted: African culture and religion were despised

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Where did the name "Uganda" come from?
questions.a: From the Kiswahili form of the word Buganda, used by the Arab and Swahili traders and later adopted by the British for the whole Protectorate.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What did the letters IBEACo stand for, and what was its work?
questions.a: The Imperial British East Africa Company. It was given a royal charter in 1888 to trade in and administer the area on behalf of Britain.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Who was Captain Lugard, and what did he do in 1890?
questions.a: He was the British officer sent by the IBEACo. In 1890 he arrived in Buganda and signed a treaty with Kabaka Mwanga, placing Buganda under the Company's protection.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: In which year did Uganda become a British Protectorate?

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name the four agreements signed in colonial Uganda and the years.
questions.a: The Buganda Agreement (1900), the Toro Agreement (1900), the Ankole Agreement (1901) and the Bunyoro Agreement (1933).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Who signed the 1900 Buganda Agreement on each side?
questions.a: Sir Harry Johnston for Britain, and the regents of the young Kabaka Daudi Chwa for Buganda.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four things contained in the 1900 Buganda Agreement.
questions.a: Any four of: Buganda accepted British protection; land was divided into mailo and Crown land; hut tax and gun tax were introduced; the Lukiiko was recognised and the Kabaka ruled under British advice; Buganda's boundaries were fixed, taking some counties from Bunyoro.
accepted: land was divided into mailo and Crown land
hut tax and gun tax were introduced
the Lukiiko was recognised and the Kabaka ruled under British advice

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is mailo land?
questions.a: Mailo land is land that was given out in square miles to the Kabaka, chiefs and notables under the 1900 Buganda Agreement.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What were the "lost counties", and why did they cause a quarrel?
questions.a: They were counties taken from Bunyoro and given to Buganda under the 1900 Agreement as a reward for helping the British. Bunyoro felt robbed, and the quarrel lasted until a referendum returned two of them to Bunyoro in 1964.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Who was Semei Kakungulu, and what did he do?
questions.a: He was a Muganda chief used by the British to bring Bukedi, Bugisu, Teso and Lango under colonial rule. He set up chiefs there on the Buganda model and founded the town of Mbale.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Which Omukama resisted the British, and what happened to him in 1899?
questions.a: Omukama Kabalega of Bunyoro. He was captured in 1899 and sent into exile, together with Kabaka Mwanga.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the ladder of colonial administration from the Governor down to the village chief.
questions.a: Governor → Provincial Commissioner → District Commissioner → County (Ssaza) chief → Sub-county (Ggombolola) chief → Parish (Muluka) chief → Village chief.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What was LEGCO, when was it formed, and when did Africans first join it?
questions.a: LEGCO was the Legislative Council, which made the laws of the Protectorate. It was formed in 1921, and the first Africans joined it in 1945.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five duties of the colonial chiefs.
questions.a: Any five of: collecting taxes; keeping law and order; settling minor cases; organising forced labour on roads; making people grow cash crops; carrying out the District Commissioner's orders.
accepted: carrying out the District Commissioner's orders

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five positive and five negative effects of Uganda becoming one nation.
questions.a: Positive: the peoples were joined into one country; peace was enforced; roads, railway, schools and hospitals were built; cash crops and trade spread; a common administration and written law came in. Negative: Uganda lost its independence; kingdoms lost power and rulers were exiled; land was given away and Bunyoro lost counties; forced labour and heavy taxes; tribal and religious divisions deepened.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six reasons why Ugandans wanted independence.
questions.a: Any six of: to rule themselves; to stop forced labour and heavy taxes; to end racial discrimination; to control their own resources; to get better prices for their crops; to restore African dignity; to get better services; the example of India and Ghana; the return of ex-soldiers; the growth of education.
accepted: to stop forced labour and heavy taxes
to get better prices for their crops
the example of India and Ghana

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six methods used in the struggle for independence.
questions.a: Any six of: forming political parties; forming cooperative societies; trade unions and strikes; boycotts; newspapers; petitions and delegations; demonstrations; constitutional conferences; taking part in elections.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name the first political party in Uganda, the year it was formed and its founder.
questions.a: The Uganda National Congress (UNC), formed in 1952 by Ignatius Kangave Musaazi.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any three other political parties, their years and their leaders.
questions.a: DP — 1954, led by Benedicto Kiwanuka; UPC — 1960, founded by Milton Obote; KY — 1961, supporters of the Kabaka.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What did the letters KY stand for, and what did the party want?
questions.a: Kabaka Yekka, meaning "the Kabaka only". It wanted to protect the position of the Kabaka and of Buganda in an independent Uganda.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Who was Benedicto Kiwanuka, and what two positions did he hold?
questions.a: He was the leader of the DP. He became the first Chief Minister in 1961 and the first Prime Minister in March 1962.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Who was Milton Obote, and what position did he hold at independence?
questions.a: He was the founder of the UPC. At independence in October 1962 he became the Prime Minister of Uganda.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What happened to Kabaka Muteesa II in 1953, and why?
questions.a: He was deported (exiled) to Britain by Governor Sir Andrew Cohen because he demanded a timetable for independence and opposed the plan for an East African federation.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: How did the Kabaka's deportation affect the struggle for independence?
questions.a: It made Ugandans very angry and united them against colonial rule; when he returned in 1955 he was a national hero, and the demand for independence became much stronger.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What was the trade boycott of 1959–60, and who led it?
questions.a: It was a refusal to buy from Asian and European shops or to use their buses, organised to force better trading chances for Africans. It was led by Augustine Kamya and the Uganda National Movement.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give the dates of internal self-government and of independence.
questions.a: Internal self-government — 1 March 1962; independence — 9 October 1962.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Where was the independence ceremony held, and what happened there?
questions.a: At Kololo in Kampala. The Union Jack was lowered and the Uganda flag was raised at midnight, and the Duke of Kent handed over the instruments of power.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Who became the first President of Uganda, and in which year?
questions.a: Sir Edward Muteesa II, in 1963, when Uganda became a republic within the Commonwealth.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six problems faced by the nationalists.
questions.a: Any six of: arrest, imprisonment and detention; deportation of leaders; banning of parties and newspapers; lack of funds and transport; disunity along religious and tribal lines; illiteracy; harsh colonial laws; fear among the people; the Buganda question.
accepted: disunity along religious and tribal lines

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw a timeline showing any six important events on Uganda's road to independence.
questions.a: Learner's timeline. Any six correct events with their years, in order — for example 1921 LEGCO, 1945 Africans in LEGCO, 1952 UNC, 1955 Kabaka returns, 1962 independence, 1963 republic.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any five national symbols of Uganda.
questions.a: Any five of: the national flag, the crested crane, the coat of arms, the national anthem, the national motto, the Constitution, the Mace.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Describe the flag of Uganda and say what each colour stands for.
questions.a: It has six stripes — black, yellow, red, black, yellow, red — with the crested crane in a white circle. Black stands for the African people, yellow for the sunshine, and red for the blood that unites all people.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is the national bird of Uganda, and what does it stand for?
questions.a: The crested crane. It stands on one leg, showing that Uganda is always moving forward, and it is a gentle, peaceful bird.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any six things shown on Uganda's coat of arms and what each represents.
questions.a: Any six: the shield and spears — defence of the country; the lion — courage; the crested crane — the nation; the waves — the lakes and rivers; the sun — sunshine; the drum — culture and tradition; coffee and cotton — agriculture.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Who composed the national anthem, and what is the national motto?
questions.a: George Wilberforce Kakoma; the motto is "For God and My Country".

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: In which year did Uganda become a republic, and who became the first President?
questions.a: In 1963; Sir Edward Muteesa II became the first President.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What happened to the kingdoms in 1967 and in 1993?
questions.a: In 1967 a new Constitution abolished the kingdoms; in 1993 they were restored as cultural institutions, without political power.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any five leaders Uganda has had since independence.
questions.a: Any five of: Sir Edward Muteesa II, Milton Obote, Idi Amin, Yusuf Lule, Godfrey Binaisa, Paulo Muwanga, Tito Okello Lutwa, Yoweri Museveni.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: In which year did the NRM take over, and on what date is it remembered?
questions.a: In 1986, remembered on 26 January as Liberation Day.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: When was the present Constitution promulgated?
questions.a: On 8 October 1995.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six achievements of independent Uganda.
questions.a: Any six of: a written Constitution and regular elections; UPE and USE; more schools, hospitals and universities; better roads, electricity and water; peace and security in most areas; growth of industry, trade and tourism; restoration of cultural institutions; membership of the EAC, AU, Commonwealth and UN; progress against HIV/AIDS.
accepted: a written Constitution and regular elections
peace and security in most areas

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six challenges facing Uganda today.
questions.a: Any six of: poverty and unemployment; rapid population growth; corruption; poor roads and few industries; diseases such as malaria and HIV/AIDS; tribalism and political conflict; insecurity and cattle rustling; environmental destruction; illiteracy; dependence on foreign aid.
accepted: diseases such as malaria and HIV/AIDS

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Suggest a solution to each of: poverty, corruption, malaria, environmental destruction.
questions.a: Poverty — skills training and support for small businesses; corruption — strong laws, accountability and punishing offenders; malaria — mosquito nets, draining stagnant water and early treatment; environmental destruction — planting trees, protecting wetlands and enforcing NEMA laws.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any five national days of Uganda and what each remembers.
questions.a: Any five: Independence Day 9 October — independence in 1962; Liberation Day 26 January — the NRM takeover; Martyrs' Day 3 June — the Uganda Martyrs; Heroes' Day 9 June — those who served the nation; Labour Day 1 May — workers; Women's Day 8 March — women.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Why is 9th October important to every Ugandan?
questions.a: Because it is the day Uganda stopped being ruled by the British and began to govern itself. It reminds every Ugandan of those who struggled for freedom and of the duty to keep the country united, peaceful and developing.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is government? Give any four reasons why a country needs one.
questions.a: Government is the group of people who make laws, carry them out and settle disputes in a country. Reasons: to make and enforce laws; to keep peace and security; to provide services; to collect and spend revenue; to protect people's rights; to represent the country abroad (any four).

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name the three arms of government and the work of each.
questions.a: Legislature (Parliament) — makes the laws; Executive — carries out the laws and runs the country; Judiciary — interprets the laws and settles disputes.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Who heads each of the three arms?
questions.a: Legislature — the Speaker; Executive — the President; Judiciary — the Chief Justice.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four duties of the President of Uganda.
questions.a: Any four of: Head of State; Head of Government; Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces; appoints ministers, judges and ambassadors; signs Bills into law; opens Parliament; represents Uganda abroad.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Describe how a Bill becomes law.
questions.a: A Bill is drafted and tabled in Parliament → it is read and debated, and studied by a committee → Parliament passes it → the President signs it → it is published and becomes an Act of Parliament.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is decentralisation?
questions.a: Decentralisation is the transfer of powers, responsibilities and services from the central government to local governments such as districts and sub-counties.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name the five levels of local council and the leader of each.
questions.a: LC I — village, Chairperson LC I; LC II — parish; LC III — sub-county; LC IV — county; LC V — district, the District Chairperson.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five duties of a local government.
questions.a: Any five of: keeping law and order; settling small disputes; running primary schools and health centres; maintaining feeder roads and water sources; collecting local revenue; planning development projects; mobilising people for immunisation and clean-ups.
accepted: running primary schools and health centres
maintaining feeder roads and water sources
mobilising people for immunisation and clean-ups

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is an election, and which body organises elections in Uganda?
questions.a: An election is the process of choosing leaders by voting. It is organised by the Electoral Commission.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Outline the steps of the electoral process.
questions.a: Registration of voters → nomination of candidates → campaigning → polling day with a secret ballot → counting the votes → declaring the results → swearing in the winners.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give the qualifications of a voter in Uganda.
questions.a: A voter must be a citizen of Uganda, 18 years or above, registered as a voter, and of sound mind.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four challenges of elections and two solutions.
questions.a: Challenges: rigging; bribery; violence and intimidation; illiteracy; late delivery of materials; low turnout (any four). Solutions: an independent Electoral Commission with a clean register and voter education; observers, agents and police at polling stations, with offenders punished and disputes settled in court.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give the four ways of becoming a citizen of Uganda.
questions.a: By birth, by descent, by registration and by naturalisation.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five rights and five responsibilities of a citizen.
questions.a: Rights (any five): life; education; property; freedom of speech, worship and association; health care; a fair trial; voting; movement. Responsibilities (any five): obeying the law; paying taxes; protecting public property and the environment; voting; respecting others' rights; keeping peace; reporting crime.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five sources of government revenue and any five ways the money is used.
questions.a: Sources (any five): taxes; licences and permits; fees for services; court fines; rent from government property; loans and grants; earnings from exports. Uses (any five): paying civil servants; building schools and hospitals; making roads and water systems; defence and security; paying debts; running Parliament and the courts; emergency relief.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Define population, population growth, population distribution and population density.
questions.a: Population — the number of people living in a place at a particular time; population growth — the increase in that number over time; population distribution — the way people are spread over an area; population density — the number of people per square kilometre.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Write the formula for population density. A district has 720,000 people and covers 9,000 km². Find its density.
questions.a: Density = total population ÷ total area. 720,000 ÷ 9,000 = 80 people per km².

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is a census? Which body carries it out in Uganda, and how often?
questions.a: A census is the official counting of all the people in a country. It is carried out by the Uganda Bureau of Statistics (UBOS), about every ten years.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give the population of Uganda according to the 2024 census.
questions.a: About 45.9 million people.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five reasons why a census is important.
questions.a: Any five of: to know the number of people and the growth rate; to plan schools, hospitals, water and roads; to plan food production and jobs; to share government services and money fairly; to plan immunisation and health services; to help investors and researchers.
accepted: to know the number of people and the growth rate
to plan food production and jobs
to share government services and money fairly
to plan immunisation and health services

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six factors that influence population distribution.
questions.a: Any six of: relief, climate, soils, vegetation, water supply, pests and diseases, transport, social services, employment and industries, security, government policy.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any three densely populated areas of Uganda and give a reason for each.
questions.a: Any three, for example: the Lake Victoria crescent — fertile soils, rainfall and jobs; Kigezi — fertile volcanic soils and a cool climate; the Elgon slopes — volcanic soils and reliable relief rainfall.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Name any three sparsely populated areas of Uganda and give a reason for each.
questions.a: Any three, for example: Karamoja — semi-arid with little water and insecurity; national parks — people are not allowed to settle there; swamps and thick forests — waterlogged or hard to clear, with pests.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any five causes of rapid population growth in Uganda.
questions.a: Any five of: high birth rate; early marriages; polygamy; low use of family planning; better health services lowering the death rate; improved food supply; cultural and religious beliefs; immigration and refugees.
accepted: better health services lowering the death rate

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any six problems caused by rapid population growth.
questions.a: Any six of: land shortage and conflicts; unemployment and poverty; pressure on schools, hospitals and water; food shortage; overcrowding and slums; poor sanitation and disease; destruction of forests and wetlands; traffic congestion; crime.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four advantages of a large population.
questions.a: Any four of: a large labour force; a bigger market for goods; more taxes for government; more ideas and skills; cheaper labour that attracts investment; development of new areas.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Suggest any six solutions to the problems of rapid population growth.
questions.a: Any six of: family planning education and services; educating girls and discouraging early marriage; creating jobs; improving farming methods; resettling people; building more social services; developing rural areas; proper town planning.
accepted: educating girls and discouraging early marriage

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: What is rural–urban migration, and give two reasons why young people move to towns?
questions.a: Rural–urban migration is the movement of people from villages to towns. Young people move to look for jobs and better pay, and for better schools, hospitals, electricity and town life.

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Give any four effects of HIV/AIDS on the population of Uganda.
questions.a: Any four of: it raised the death rate, especially among young working adults; it left many orphans and child-headed families; it reduced the labour force; it increased costs for families and government; it lowered the population growth rate for a time.
accepted: it left many orphans and child-headed families
it increased costs for families and government
it lowered the population growth rate for a time

questions.subject: SST
questions.q: Draw the map of Uganda and shade one densely and one sparsely populated area, giving a reason for each.
questions.a: Learner's map. For example, the Lake Victoria crescent shaded as densely populated because of fertile soils and jobs, and Karamoja shaded as sparsely populated because it is semi-arid.
